demo-1-play-a-registry-from-creation-to-.text: Demo 1: play a registry from creation to termination.

As a Cardano developer who knows wallets, faucets and Koios but has never used Singular, you want to watch a registry work before you read how it is built: a registry is created, a key is put in it, changed and ended, the registry refuses what it must refuse, and two people sign their writes in two different ways. Demo 1 is that play, in sixteen steps. The steps, and the programs to run them, live in a repository of their own, singular-demo. This page says what the play shows and where to play it.

what-the-play-shows.text: Two people, Alice and Bob, share one registry. Its application, open datum, lets a key carry a payload that only the key's controller may replace, and keeps a deposit of 2 tADA with the key until the key is terminated.

The play creates the registry, books a key and folds it so that the key becomes active, updates its payload, books and folds the key's end, then rejects a request that nobody folded, reclaims a new one inside its retract window, and books and folds one more key.

A write does not change the registry at once. It books a request, which waits until someone folds it, and any wallet may fold. A request that nobody folds within its processing window can be rejected once a second window, the retract window, has also passed; inside that second window its owner can take it back. The play walks each of these, so that you see the refusals where they happen: a reject that comes too early is refused, and so is a reclaim that comes too early.

The two people sign in the two ways Singular offers. Alice names her vault, a file holding her signing key sealed by a passphrase, and one command builds, signs and sends. Bob names only his wallet's address and a bundle file: the command builds the transactions into the file, signs nothing, and exits with status 19, which means it is waiting for signatures. Then Bob signs the bundle from his vault and sends it, so the machine that builds a write never needs to hold the key.

where-to-play-it.text: Every way below plays the same sixteen steps. The table lists three: the step-by-step page to paste from, which needs the programs, and the Nix shell and the Ubuntu kit, which are two ways to get the programs. Start with the step-by-step page.
The singular-demo repository describes the shell and the kit, what each is pinned to and what it was tested on.

what-it-does-not-claim.text: Everything the step-by-step page runs happens on a private test chain that it starts; nothing touches a public network. The open datum application protects the payload and the deposit and nothing more: it demonstrates the registry's mechanics. The receipts of a play are evidence of behaviour on a private chain only, and no complete conformance is claimed here. What the project does claim, and what it leaves open, is on the conformance evidence page. What is deployed on the public preprod network, and the transactions the project's own journeys submitted there, are recorded in the preprod record.

the-release-behind-it.text: The play runs a release of Singular. These pages are about the release itself, not about the steps: install the commands without Nix and download and verify a release. Each release archive also carries the same story as a run page, DEMO1.md (the page in the repository), which builds the commands from the archive and which the project's hosted checks run against every change.
